analysis.one_liner: Replaced guaranteed federal cash aid for poor families with five-year, work-ruled state block grants and cut food stamps, disability benefits, and aid to immigrants.
analysis.headline: Congress ended the 60-year federal guarantee of cash aid to poor families, imposing work rules and five-year lifetime limits; it passed the House 328-101 and the Senate 78-21, and President Clinton signed it into law on August 22, 1996.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill replaced the Aid to Families with Dependent Children program — an entitlement guaranteeing cash aid to eligible poor families — with fixed block grants to states (TANF) that end after five years and require parents to work. It tightened food stamp rules (jobless adults generally limited to three months of benefits in three years), narrowed disability benefits for poor children, barred most legal immigrants from major federal aid for five years, and strengthened child support enforcement. It also gave states wide freedom to design their own programs and to contract with private and religious organizations to deliver services.
analysis.who_benefits: State governments, which received fixed federal funding with wide discretion and no open-ended federal match; the federal budget, which converted open-ended spending into fixed block grants; custodial parents owed child support, who gained stronger enforcement tools (new-hire directories, automatic wage withholding, license and passport penalties); and low-income families moving from welfare to work in a strong economy, who kept 12 months of Medicaid after leaving cash aid and gained child care block grant funding.
analysis.who_benefits_short: State governments, federal budget, child-support recipients

how_it_helps.text: States receive fixed block grants and may use them flexibly, including for child care, heating aid, job placement, and individual development accounts for home purchase, education, or starting a business.

The bill requires states to move welfare parents into work, with minimum participation rates rising to 50 percent of all families and 90 percent of two-parent families, and preserves 12 months of Medicaid for families who leave welfare for work.

It strengthens child support enforcement with statewide new-hire directories, automatic income withholding, credit reporting of arrears, license suspension, passport denial, and nondischargeability of child support debts in bankruptcy.
It consolidates child care funding into a block grant and lets states contract with charitable, religious, and private organizations to deliver services.

analysis.who_pays: Poor families bear the main cost: the individual entitlement to cash aid is ended, aid is generally limited to five years in a lifetime, and states can sanction families by cutting payments for not meeting work or other requirements. Jobless childless adults can be cut off food stamps after three months; most legal immigrants lose SSI, food stamps, TANF, and Medicaid eligibility; children receiving disability benefits face a stricter eligibility standard and periodic redeterminations; and families with drug felony convictions can be banned for life unless a state opts out.
analysis.who_pays_short: Poor families, disabled children, legal immigrants

drawbacks.text: The bill formally terminates entitlements to AFDC and JOBS benefits effective October 1, 1996, and states that no individual is entitled to assistance under a state TANF program, ending a guaranteed floor of cash support for children in poor families.

Food stamps become unavailable to jobless adults without children for more than three months in any 36-month period unless working at least 20 hours a week, with exemptions only in limited situations.
Most legal immigrants are made ineligible for SSI, food stamps, TANF, social services block grants, and Medicaid, and non-qualified aliens are barred from most federal and state benefits.

The bill narrows the definition of disability for poor children to 'marked and severe functional limitations,' ends individualized functional assessments, and requires periodic continuing disability reviews and redeterminations at age 18.
Individuals convicted of drug felonies after enactment are barred from TANF and food stamps, along with other family members, unless a state opts out.

The House voted 418-0 to instruct conferees to eliminate provisions that shift costs to states and increase child poverty and to protect food stamps and Medicaid, but the final conference report retained the block grant structure and benefit restrictions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill did succeed at cutting the cash welfare rolls sharply and, in the strong late-1990s economy, moving many parents into work, and it gave states flexibility and real child support enforcement gains. But the costs are serious and fall entirely on people with little power to object: a hard five-year lifetime limit means families who exhaust it have nothing when jobs disappear, the food stamp cutoff hits jobless childless adults with no alternative income, and the immigrant and childhood-disability cuts took benefits from people with no connection to work requirements. The design is risky by construction — block grants are fixed regardless of recessions — and the one safeguard Congress included for children in poverty is a non-binding sense-of-Congress resolution.

outcome.mechanism: Both chambers passed it with large bipartisan majorities in July 1996, a conference committee kept the benefit cuts intact, and President Clinton signed it on August 22, 1996, making it Public Law 104-193.

narrative.text: Introduced on June 27, 1996, the bill was reported by the House Budget Committee as an original reconciliation measure under the fiscal year 1997 budget resolution.
The House passed it on July 18, 1996 by a vote of 256-170, with 226 of 235 Republicans in favor and 30 of 198 Democrats.

Before passage, a Democratic motion to recommit the bill with instructions to eliminate provisions shifting costs to states and increasing child poverty failed 203-220, with 195 of 198 Democrats in favor and 220 of 234 Republicans opposed.
The Senate passed its own version in lieu of S. 1956 on July 23, 1996 by a vote of 74-24, with 51 of 53 Republicans and 23 of 47 Democrats in favor.
On July 24 the House voted 418-0, with no member opposed, to instruct conferees to remove provisions that shift costs to states, increase child poverty, or cut food stamps and Medicaid coverage.

The House agreed to the conference report 328-101 on July 31, with 230 of 235 Republicans and exactly half of Democrats (98 of 198) in favor, and the Senate agreed 78-21 on August 1, with 53 of 53 Republicans and 25 of 47 Democrats.
President Clinton presented and signed the bill on August 22, 1996, and it became Public Law 104-193, the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments came out ahead, gaining decades of guaranteed block grants with broad discretion and none of the open-ended federal match; the federal budget gained fixed, capped costs. Families who lost benefits — especially jobless childless adults, legal immigrants, and disabled children — bore the cost.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State governments and the federal budget

sides.party_line_note: Republicans backed the bill almost unanimously (226 of 235 House, 51-53 of 53 Senate), while Democrats split — most opposed the first House vote (30 of 198 in favor) but half joined to pass the final conference report (98 House Democrats, 25 Senate Democrats).

industries.note: The bill converts open-ended federal matching funds into fixed block grants and gives states broad discretion over eligibility, sanctions, and time limits. States gain guaranteed funding and flexibility, but they also absorb the risk when recessions increase the caseload and the fixed grant does not grow.

industries.industry: Private social service and child care providers, including religious organizations
industries.note: The bill authorizes states to contract with charitable, religious, and private organizations to deliver welfare services and removes the nonprofit requirement for child care providers, routing block grant funds through these providers. Recipients receive services, but faith-based providers may deliver them subject to a ban on using funds for worship or proselytizing.

The bill directs states to implement electronic benefit transfer for food stamps and TANF and exempts these systems from several consumer protections under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act. Payment processors and financial institutions gain business while benefit recipients lose some standard error-resolution protections.
